notes.meaning: Bezalel built the large outdoor altar where animal sacrifices would be offered to God. It was a square chest made of acacia wood and covered in bronze so it could bear the heat of the fire. At each of its four corners, he carved a horn-shaped point that formed one piece with the altar. This altar was the place where people approached God to seek forgiveness through sacrifice.

All the tools used at the altar were also cast from bronze. These included buckets to carry away ashes, shovels to stir the fire, basins to hold blood, meat forks, and pans for carrying hot coals. Every utensil had a practical role in caring for the sacred fire and keeping the altar clean.

Bezalel made a bronze grating that rested inside the altar halfway up from the bottom. This mesh allowed ashes to drop through while holding the burning wood in place. At the four corners of the grate, he cast bronze rings to hold the carrying poles.

The carrying poles were carved from acacia wood and coated with bronze. The workers slipped the poles through the side rings so the altar could be lifted without anyone touching it. The altar was constructed from wooden boards so it remained hollow and light enough to move during travel.

The large washing basin and its base were made from polished bronze mirrors given by devout women who gathered at the entrance of the tent. In those days, mirrors were crafted from shiny, smoothed metal instead of glass. These women gave up their personal beauty items for God's house, providing the basin where priests washed their hands and feet to be cleansed before serving.

Bezalel set up the enclosed courtyard around the tabernacle tent. The south wall was about one hundred and fifty feet long, formed by hanging curtains of fine white linen on twenty pillars. These pillars stood in heavy bronze bases and were linked at the top with silver hooks and connecting rods.

The north wall of the courtyard was built just like the south wall, with twenty pillars and white linen curtains. The west end and the east end were each about seventy-five feet wide, supported by ten pillars each. These linen walls kept the courtyard distinct and separate from the rest of the camp.

On the east side, where the entrance was placed, curtains hung on both sides of the gate, each supported by three pillars. The entire perimeter was surrounded by curtains of finely spun linen. This bright white border reminded everyone who approached that God is pure and holy.

The posts stood securely in bronze sockets set in the dirt, while their tops and bands were covered with silver. This silver trim tied the fence together and gave it a bright, finished appearance. Using valuable metals on the outer fence showed that even the courtyard was dedicated to God.

The gate curtain for the courtyard was thirty feet wide and brightly embroidered with blue, purple, and red yarn on fine linen. It hung from four posts set into bronze bases with silver hooks and trim. Its bright colors marked the single doorway through which people could come toward God's presence.

All the tent pegs used to stake down both the tabernacle tent and the courtyard fence were made of bronze. Bronze was tough enough to be driven into the desert ground and resist rust. This ensured that the entire structure remained sturdy during strong wilderness winds.

Moses ordered a complete inventory of the metals used to build the tabernacle of the Testimony, where God's law was kept. Aaron's son Ithamar led the Levites in counting and recording the weights. Keeping an open record proved that all the gifts brought by the people were handled honestly.

Bezalel led the master craftsmen, carefully obeying every instruction the Lord had given to Moses. He was assisted by Oholiab, who was specially skilled in engraving, designing, and weaving fine colored textiles. God gave these men both the creative skill and the faithfulness to finish the work well.

The total gold freely given by the people weighed over a ton according to the official sanctuary weights. This gold was used to make the sacred furniture, the golden lampstand, and the holy vessels inside the tent. The Israelites had carried this gold from Egypt, and they gladly offered it back to God.

The silver came from the half-shekel ransom money required from every adult man during the census. A total of 603,550 men were counted, which yielded more than five tons of silver. Because rich and poor paid the exact same half-shekel, it showed that all people have equal standing and need the same redemption before God.

The workers melted one talent of silver for each of the one hundred heavy base sockets of the sanctuary walls and inner curtain. The remaining silver was shaped into hooks, top plates, and bands for the courtyard posts. In this way, the tabernacle literally rested upon the silver given for the people's redemption.

The bronze brought as a wave offering weighed about two and a half tons. The craftsmen used it to cast the altar of burnt offering, its utensils, the courtyard post sockets, and all the tent pegs. This sturdy metal was chosen for the items exposed to daily heat and outdoor weather.
